message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition.
• Repairs for health and safety issues must be made promptly. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but do so only after following the proper procedure. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments.
• If you’re late, notify the landlord in writing and ask for a grace period if possible. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without notice (usually 24–48 hrs) except in emergencies. | • Ask for written notice of any planned entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, document incidents and consider filing a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a lease with proper notice (typically 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a written notice of termination. | • Review your lease for specific notice requirements. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Keep copies of all correspondence. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the correct procedure (e.g., give notice, keep receipts). | • Document the problem, send a written notice, and keep receipts. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must respect your privacy and cannot harass or threaten you. | • Report any harassment to local authorities or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in writing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlords may inspect the unit for maintenance or safety reasons, but must give reasonable notice. | • Ask for a written notice of inspection. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If your rights are violated, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or pursue civil action in court. | • Keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – For repairs, entry, and termination. 4. **Keep Copies of All Correspondence** – Emails, letters, and notices. 5. **Know When to Seek Legal Help** – If you face eviction, discrimination, or serious habitability issues. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | File complaints about landlord‑tenant disputes. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | | **Texas Property Code** | The statutory law governing landlord‑tenant relationships. | Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific point or if you’d like help drafting a notice or understanding a particular clause in your lease.
